source: Russell and Wefald (1991) Do the Right Thing: Studies in Limited Rationality
finding: Founding text. Treats each computation as an action. Its value is the expected gain in decision quality minus the time cost. Stop when no computation has positive net value. Myopic (one-step) estimates make it practical.
numbers: Not read this session (search tools were out of quota). Book reports game-tree search tests; exact figures not verified.
limits: Myopic estimates can stop too early when one step looks useless but several together would help. Book not opened; details unverified.
agent_relevance: Gives the rule for the S0 gate and S6 trigger: spend more thinking only if expected gain exceeds cost.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (RaM)
finding: Trains an LLM with a reward equal to the gain in answer log-probability from a reasoning chain minus a per-token cost (a direct copy of the value-of-computation formula). The model learns to think less on easy items.
numbers: Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; 4096 training items (1024 each from ARC, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K, ProofWriter); K=4 chains, lambda=0.1. Abstract: 23-45% fewer tokens than few-shot CoT with equal or better accuracy. 23-32% fewer output tokens than STaR. On MMLU-CF out of distribution: 28-36% fewer tokens than STaR with similar accuracy.
quote: VOC = expected gain in best action value minus cost(c)
limits: Small base models, closed-answer tasks; agentic settings untested (authors say so). The gain term uses the gold answer, so it is a training signal, not a runtime rule.
agent_relevance: Evidence the value-of-computation form works as a training reward. At runtime our program needs a proxy for the gain term.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2025) RaM, adaptivity and domain results
finding: RaM widens the length gap between hard and easy problems. Instruction-tuned models did not adapt length to difficulty. Reasoning helped mainly on maths and logic, little on fact recall.
numbers: Hard/easy split by whether direct few-shot answering failed. Length gap grew from CoT few-shot to STaR to RaM (table values garbled in text extraction, not recorded). Physics and engineering subjects shrank less than recall subjects (Fig. 3).
limits: Split depends on the base model's own direct accuracy.
agent_relevance: Supports gating by difficulty signal: skip long thinking where a direct answer already works.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2018) Learning to select computations (BMPS)
finding: Bayesian metalevel policy search learns a near-optimal rule for which computation to run, using two features: myopic value of information and value of perfect information.
numbers: Domain 1: BMPS at most 5.19% below optimal; 6.78-35.8% better than meta-greedy (20.3% on average). Domain 3: BMPS 0.6535 vs optimal 0.6596 (99.1%); meta-greedy 0.60; full deliberation 0.20; DQN 0.58.
limits: Small simulated metalevel problems with known reward structure, not natural language.
agent_relevance: A cheap two-feature rule beats always-think (0.20) and one-step greedy (0.60). Template for a coded S6 trigger.

source: Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony (2012) Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications
finding: Formal theory of choosing which simulations to run. Shows the myopic policy can fail in selection problems and gives new heuristic policies. Applied to flat selection and Monte Carlo tree search in Go.
numbers: Abstract claims the new policies outperform earlier published methods for flat selection and Go; exact win rates not extracted.
limits: Optimal metalevel policy is hard; heuristics only. UCT's bandit rule ignores computation cost.
agent_relevance: Warns that a one-step value check can undervalue a thinking step that pays off only in combination.

source: Lin, Kolobov, Kamar, Horvitz (2015) Metareasoning for Planning Under Uncertainty
finding: Formal metareasoning for online planning in MDPs. Optimal general metareasoning is at most polynomially harder than the base planning problem, but impractical. Reasoning about when to stop reasoning raises infinite regress.
numbers: Theory result plus approximate procedures; numbers not extracted.
limits: Optimal rule too costly to run; approximations needed.
agent_relevance: The gate must itself be cheap code. A model that deliberates about whether to deliberate is the regress case.

source: Arora and Zanette (2025) Training Language Models to Reason Efficiently
finding: RL with a length penalty (one knob alpha) trades tokens for accuracy. Savings are larger on easy sets.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill 1.5B and 7B. 7B: about 50% fewer tokens with under 5% accuracy loss. AIME24: 16% fewer tokens, -3.3 points. MATH500: 37% fewer, -2.2. GSM8K: 65% fewer, -1.7. Another setting: 27% saving on AIME24, 83% on GSM8K.
limits: Math only; needs training. Cost term is token count, not value-aware.
agent_relevance: Shows the easy-versus-hard asymmetry that a difficulty gate should exploit.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models burn many tokens on trivial questions, with extra solutions that add little accuracy or diversity. Self-training that removes redundant solutions cuts tokens.
numbers: For 'what is 2 plus 3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one QwQ answer had 13 solutions. Token cut of 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview at same accuracy. Outcome efficiency under 50% on the easiest MATH level.
limits: Two model families (QwQ, R1 distills); metrics defined by the authors.
agent_relevance: Models do not meter thinking by difficulty. An external gate is needed.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: The opposite error. On hard problems o1-like models switch between ideas too often. Wrong answers contain more thought switches and more tokens than right ones. A decoding penalty on switching words (TIP) raises accuracy without fine-tuning.
numbers: AIME2024 and two other hard sets with QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1; conventional models show no length gap between right and wrong answers. Exact TIP gains not extracted.
limits: Needs decoding access, so not usable on a closed API agent.
agent_relevance: Overthinking and underthinking both occur. A value rule must say 'continue this line' as well as 'stop'.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally
finding: Best use of test-time compute depends on question difficulty. Choosing the method per difficulty bin beats uniform best-of-N.
numbers: PaLM-2 on MATH. Compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute (64 versus 256 samples). Beam search wins on harder questions and low budgets; best-of-N wins on easy questions and high budgets.
limits: Difficulty bins used ground truth or a model-estimated proxy with 2-fold cross-validation; PaLM-2 fine-tuned for revision.
agent_relevance: Numeric case for a difficulty-conditioned S0 gate, and for switching method, not just amount.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: cut thinking at a token cap or append 'Wait' to extend it. Extending gave more accuracy up to a point.
numbers: s1-32B (1,000 training examples) beats o1-preview by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24. AIME24 rises from 50% to 57% with budget forcing.
limits: Forced extension is a fixed rule, not value-driven. Later work shows decline after more thinking.
agent_relevance: A cheap control knob exists, but it is a schedule, which G1 forbids unless tied to a signal.

source: Qu, Yang, Setlur et al. (2025) Optimizing Test-Time Compute via Meta Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (MRT)
finding: Frames test-time compute as meta-RL with cumulative regret over output blocks. Adds a dense bonus equal to the progress each block makes in the chance of final success: a learned per-step value of computation.
numbers: Abstract: 2-3x relative gain in performance and about 1.5x token efficiency over outcome-reward RL on math; state of the art at 1.5B scale on AIME24/25, AMC23 and others. Authors state current frontier models do not minimise regret.
limits: Training-time method; progress estimated with rollouts.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable signal: change in estimated success chance per thinking block. Stop when progress is near zero.

source: Probing hidden states for self-verification: Reasoning Models Know When They're Right (2025)
finding: A small probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct. Used as an early-exit rule.
numbers: Confidence-thresholded early exit cut inference tokens by up to 24% with no accuracy loss.
limits: Needs internal activations; math-style tasks.
agent_relevance: Confidence signals exist inside the model. For API agents use an external check or answer agreement instead.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models
finding: Training-free early exit. At reasoning transition points, probe a trial answer and stop if the model is confident.
numbers: 10 benchmarks, 11 reasoning models: chain length cut by 19.1% to 80.1% on average while accuracy changed by +0.3% to +5.0%.
limits: Uses model confidence, which can be overconfident; savings vary 4x across models.
agent_relevance: A runtime rule of the 'stop when more thinking is low value' kind. Accuracy rose, so overthinking costs accuracy as well as time.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking (NoThinking)
finding: Skipping the thinking block can match or beat thinking at equal token budgets, and parallel NoThinking samples with best-of-N are strong.
numbers: At 700 tokens on AMC23: 51.3 (NoThinking) vs 28.9 (Thinking). Parallel NoThinking comparable to Thinking at up to 9x lower latency.
limits: Distilled R1 models; gap shrinks as budget grows; pass@k framing.
agent_relevance: At low budgets, many cheap attempts beat one long chain. Fits the parallel-then-select design in G4/G5.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: RL teaches a reasoning model to choose NoThinking or Thinking per problem. NoThinking is better for simple tasks.
numbers: GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24: average response length down 53.0% (1.5B) and 40.1% (7B); accuracy up 2.4% and 2.3%.
limits: Training needed; math only.
agent_relevance: Learned S0 gate: skipping thinking on easy items raised accuracy as well as saving tokens.

source: Fang, Ma, Wang (2025) Thinkless: LLM Learns When to Think
finding: One model emits a control token (think or short) first, trained with decoupled GRPO. Plain GRPO collapsed the mode choice early.
numbers: Reduces long-chain thinking by 50-90% on Minerva Algebra, MATH-500 and GSM8K (abstract).
limits: Mode-collapse risk; decision depends on model ability and query.
agent_relevance: The 'think or not' choice is learnable but unstable. Prefer a coded gate to a learned one.

source: Meta-Reasoner: Dynamic Guidance for Optimized Inference-time Reasoning in LLMs (2025, v6 2026)
finding: A contextual bandit reads the reasoning progress and picks a strategy (continue, backtrack, switch, restart). A metalevel policy for an LLM.
numbers: Claims 9-12% higher accuracy than prior methods on Game-of-24, TheoremQA, SciBench; about 51-55% less inference time than o1-preview at comparable performance.
limits: Progress summary is written by the LLM, so the state signal is model-judged. Removing the bandit hurt most when it fell back to plain CoT.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to an S6 trigger inside an LLM loop. Make the progress signal code-measured.

source: Learning When to Plan: Efficiently Allocating Test-Time Compute for LLM Agents (2025, v3 2026)
finding: In agent tasks, planning before every action (ReAct style) is costly and hurts on long horizons. Never planning also hurts. Best is an intermediate plan frequency.
numbers: Crafter and POGS. Fine-tuned 8B agent (SFT+RL) reward 0.387 vs Llama-3.3-70B zero-shot 0.379 with 85% fewer tokens. Plan completion 20% vs 16% for SFT only; discards plans via replanning 41% vs 35%. Gemini 2.5 Flash dropped markedly when always planning on Crafter.
limits: Two environments; reward gap vs 70B is small (0.008). Always-plan agents backtracked most and had lower success.
agent_relevance: Direct agent-loop evidence for G1: forced per-step deliberation is worse than signal-driven deliberation.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT?
finding: Meta-analysis of when chain-of-thought helps. Large gains only on symbolic, maths and logic tasks.
numbers: 110 papers, 1,218 comparisons. Mean CoT gains: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9 points. Top three task types: 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. Other categories: 56.8 vs 56.1.
limits: Meta-analysis of reported deltas, mixed prompts and models.
agent_relevance: Basis for a task-type gate: skip written reasoning for knowledge-type questions.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, asking the model to revise its own answer does not help and often hurts. A model-judged revise step has negative value.
limits: Intrinsic correction only; gains reappear with oracle labels or tool feedback.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: a self-critique pass has negative expected value unless tied to real output.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Accuracy rises then falls as thinking is extended (for example with 'Wait'). The authors explain the rise as higher output variance, not better reasoning. Parallel thinking with majority vote does better at the same budget.
numbers: Parallel thinking up to 20% higher accuracy than extended thinking at the same inference budget.
limits: Explanation rests on a simple probabilistic model fitted by the authors.
agent_relevance: Value of computation is non-monotone. A stop rule must exist; a fixed extension schedule is risky.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
finding: Built tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy. Five failure modes: distraction by irrelevant detail (Claude), overfitting to framing (o-series), drift to spurious correlations, loss of focus on deduction, amplified concerning behaviour.
numbers: Task families: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction (zebra puzzles), AI-risk probes. No aggregate effect size extracted.
limits: Tasks are designed to expose failure, so not typical workloads.
agent_relevance: Marginal value of computation can be negative. Supports a hard cap and stop-on-no-progress.

source: Damani, Shenfeld, Peng, Bobu, Andreas (2024) Learning How Hard to Think
finding: Predict the reward distribution for an input and budget, then give more samples to inputs where extra compute helps most, or route to a cheap or costly decoder.
numbers: Code, maths, dialog: same quality with up to 50% less compute, or up to 10% better quality at fixed compute. Many coding problems have 0% success, so extra compute there is wasted.
limits: Needs a trained difficulty predictor; gains differ by task (code up to 50%, chat about 10%).
agent_relevance: Marginal-value allocation across items. Hopeless items should get a default answer.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stop sampling when the majority lead is statistically safe (Dirichlet model). A coded value-of-more-samples rule.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, 3 LLMs: up to 7.9x fewer samples, average accuracy drop under 0.1%.
limits: Assumes samples are independent; same-model samples are correlated (our G4).
agent_relevance: Ready-made coded stopping rule for the sampling stage. Treat agreement as a hint only.

source: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), ICLR 2024
finding: Sample in small windows; stop when a window is unanimous.
numbers: Average sampling cut: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8% (more sets in paper), accuracy kept; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-2 7B.
limits: Same independence caveat; savings largest on easy sets.
agent_relevance: Same pattern: savings concentrate where problems are easy.

source: Chen, Zaharia, Zou (2023) FrugalGPT
finding: Cascade of models: ask the cheap model first and escalate only if a scorer is not confident.
numbers: Up to 98% cost reduction at GPT-4 accuracy, or up to 4% higher accuracy at the same cost.
limits: Needs a trained answer scorer; results on selected datasets.
agent_relevance: An escalate-on-low-confidence gate. Similar logic could trigger S6.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: fast and slow thinking agent
finding: Agent with a cheap fast module and a costly deliberate module, switched by coded rules.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 tasks: score 84.7 vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3. Tokens per action 757 vs 1,856 (SayCan), 1,971 (ReAct), 2,983 (Reflexion).
limits: Switching rule is hand-written; one benchmark family; the small module is fine-tuned on oracle trajectories.
agent_relevance: A coded trigger for deliberation beat always deliberating at under half the tokens.

source: Zilberstein and Horvitz line: anytime algorithms and bounded optimality (1987-2011)
finding: Classic AI line: anytime algorithms with performance profiles, and the rule to stop when marginal gain per second falls below its cost.
numbers: No figures verified; sources not opened.
limits: Recalled from memory; do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Supports a marginal-gain stop rule using measured progress, not a clock.

source: Pan et al. (2025) Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively
finding: In Little Alchemy 2 most LLMs explore worse than humans. Models rely on uncertainty cues; humans also use empowerment. Sparse autoencoder analysis suggests uncertainty is encoded early and empowerment late, so models decide before the later value signal arrives.
numbers: Abstract: most LLMs underperform humans except o1; the DeepSeek reasoning model with longer thought was closer to human exploration. Counts not extracted.
limits: One game; interpretation from SAE probing.
agent_relevance: Too little thinking also loses on open-ended tasks. The gate needs a floor for exploration tasks.

source: Thinking vs. Doing: Agents that Reason by Scaling Test-Time Interaction (2025)
finding: Scaling the number of interaction steps, not thinking tokens, lets web agents explore and re-plan. Prompting alone helped; a curriculum RL method (TTI) trained rollout length adaptively.
numbers: Gemma 3 12B with TTI reported state of the art among open web agents in the abstract; numbers not extracted.
limits: Web benchmarks only.
agent_relevance: Value of computation can be spent on acting and observing, which brings real information, instead of thinking.
